PR 190 fix(semantic): read a relation endpoint's path out of the ID correctly https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/190
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/111
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## The bug

`semanticEndpointPath` derived a file path from a semantic relation endpoint ID with `strings.Split(id, ":")` and returned `parts[2]`. That path is what `.brainignore` is matched against.

entire-graph builds endpoint IDs by joining **unescaped** fields with `":"`:

```
symbol:   <repo-key>:<language>:<path>:<kind>:<qualified-name>
file:     <repo-key>:file:<path>
external: external:<kind>:<value>
```

Three of those fields may legitimately contain `":"` — a file path (`od:d/mod.py`), a local repo key (`local/<directory name>`), and a qualified name (an Express route symbol is named `/users/:id`). So the fixed-index read landed on the wrong segment:

| case | endpoint | path read |
|---|---|---|
| ordinary | `main.go` | `main.go` — ok |
| colon in the **file path**, ordinary repo | `od:d/mod.py` | `od` — wrong |
| colon in the **repo key** | `main.go` | `Go` — wrong |

**No unusual directory name is needed.** An ordinary GitHub-keyed repo containing a file at `od:d/mod.py` is enough, and the `len(parts) < 5` guard does not fire (that ID splits into six fields).

### Two data-integrity consequences

1. **Relations redacted for files that are not ignored.** With a `.brainignore` rule for the directory `od`, `od:d/mod.py` is correctly kept — the file record and its symbols survive, because those are filtered by their real `file_path`. But every relation touching them was dropped, because the endpoint parse read `"od"`. One-sided, silent loss of the relation graph for a file the user never asked to hide. The stock ignore set (`build`, `vendor`, `dist`, `target`, `node_modules`) reaches this with no `.brainignore` at all: a file at `build:tools/mod.go` keeps its symbols and loses its edges.

2. **Relations kept for files that are ignored.** A file endpoint has three fields, so `len(parts) < 5` returned `""` for *every* file endpoint and skipped the check entirely. entire-graph resolves imports and co-change pairs to `<repo-key>:file:<path>` endpoints for files it emits no record for, so the ignored-ID set cannot cover them and the endpoint ID is the only signal — a relation naming `secret/config.go` went into the brain verbatim.

The function's own comment encoded the false premise ("the repo key, language, and kind segments never contain `:`, so the path is always the third field").

## The fix

A relation record has no `file_path` to read the path off: entire-graph's `RelationRecord` carries only `from_id`/`to_id`. The path has to come out of the ID, so the parse is now anchored on the two fields that are known to be free of `":"`.

- **The repo key.** The snapshot header carries it, and entire-graph builds the header field and every ID from the same value (`sc.key`), so the prefix match is exact. An endpoint carrying a different repo key names no file in this repository and now resolves to no path rather than a spurious one.
- **The kind**, which is always a bare token — no `"/"`, no `"."`.

A **file** endpoint is then exact by construction: everything after the `file:` marker is the path, colons included. A **symbol** endpoint cuts the language at the first colon and takes the first split whose kind field is a bare token — which keeps a colon in the qualified name from stealing the split (`route` is accepted before `/users/:id` can be read as a kind) while stepping over one in the path (`d/mod.py` is rejected as a kind, so `od:d/mod.py` stays whole).

Escaping or sanitising the repo key was not the fix here: the path injects colons through the same joint, so the consumer stays broken regardless.

## Tests

`internal/cli/semantic_endpoint_path_test.go`:

- `TestSemanticEndpointPathRecoversFieldsAroundColons` — 15 cases across every ID shape: colon in the path, in the repo key, in the qualified name, in the path *and* the qualified name, file endpoints with and without a colon, externals, a foreign repo key, an opaque endpoint.
- `TestSemanticIndexKeepsRelationsForColonPathOutsideIgnoredDirectory` — end to end through `runSemanticIndex` with a real `.brainignore`: a rule for `od` must not redact `od:d/mod.py`.
- `TestSemanticIndexDropsRelationsForIgnoredColonPath` — the same path, genuinely ignored, is redacted.
- `TestSemanticIndexDropsRelationsToIgnoredFileEndpoints` — relations naming ignored files only through file endpoint IDs are dropped and their paths do not appear in the persisted snapshot.
- `TestFilterSemanticSnapshotHonorsColonPathEndpoints` — the re-filter path shares the parse and reaches the same verdicts.

`TestSemanticEndpointPath` is retired in place; the new table covers all six of its cases.

**Mutation-verified.** Restoring the `strings.Split` body behind the new signature (so it still compiles) fails four of the five tests, reproducing the exact wrong values above — `"od"` for `od:d/mod.py`, `"Go"` for the colon-in-repo-key case, `""` for every file endpoint.

`go test ./internal/cli -run 'Semantic|Ignore|Relation' -count=1` green; `go vet ./...` and `gofmt` clean.

## Known residual

The kind anchor cannot separate a path whose colon-delimited tail segment is itself a bare token — a file literally named `od:README` still resolves to `od`. Closing that would mean pinning entire-graph's kind enum inside Brain, trading a contrived case for a drift hazard on every kind the provider adds. Every path shape with a `/` or a `.` after the colon — which is every path with a directory or an extension — resolves exactly.

PR 188 fix(mcp): bound brain_index_repository the way brain_refresh is bounded https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/188
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/109
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## The defect

`runMCP` serves one request at a time: read a frame, handle it to completion, write the response, read again. However long a tool call takes is time the server answers **nothing at all** — not another tool, not a host's liveness check.

`brain_refresh` already carries an MCP-scoped deadline for exactly that reason, with a comment saying so and an error pointing at the CLI. `brain_index_repository` — the one tool that walks the whole repository through an external provider, so the one most able to run long — had none. It ran on the bare request context.

## Measured

Against the built binary on this repository (40,818 symbols, 131,677 relations), three requests written back to back into the same stdio pipe:

```
t=+ 0.0s  initialize            -> answered
t=+40.0s  brain_index_repository-> answered
t=+42.3s  brain_status          -> answered
```

`brain_status` was sitting in the pipe the whole time. Nothing came back for 40 seconds. That is longer than a typical host tool-call timeout, and on a larger repository — or with a provider that wedges — there is no ceiling at all.

## The change

Wrap the index in `mcpIndexTimeout` and convert a deadline into the same shape of error `brain_refresh` returns, naming the CLI command that has no such constraint. The provider runs under `exec.CommandContext`, so the deadline actually reclaims the pipe rather than just abandoning the wait.

The value matches `mcpRefreshTimeout` deliberately: the constraint is not about how long indexing "should" take, it is about how long a single MCP call may hold the only pipe. Both are `var`s so tests can shrink them.

## Tests

`TestMCPBrainIndexRepositoryHonorsTimeout` shrinks the bound to 1ms, runs the index against a runner that blocks until its context is cancelled, and asserts both halves: the timeout is surfaced to the caller, **and the request queued behind it is then served** — the pipe came back, which is the whole point.

Mutation-verified: dropping the deadline compiles, and the test then **hangs until the Go test timeout** (`FAIL ... 60.523s`) rather than failing fast — which is precisely the defect. Restoring passes in 0.6s.

## Gating

Run locally — the org's Actions billing limit was reached, so CI may not start.

- `go test ./internal/cli -run TestMCP -count=1` — 57 passed
- `gofmt`, `go vet ./internal/cli` clean

## Scope

One tool's context. No overlap with the other open MCP PRs (#117, #118, #133, #156, #157, #158, #185, #186, #187).

Not addressed here, and noted for the record: the serial request loop itself. Making the server handle concurrent tool calls is a design change — the per-response privacy lock handoff (`mcpResponsePrivacyState`) and the brain's file locks both assume one in-flight request — so this PR bounds the worst offender rather than reworking the loop.

PR 187 fix(mcp): stop emitting a result frame the server would refuse to read https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/187
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/108
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## The defect

`readMCPMessage` rejects an **inbound** frame over `maxMCPFrameBytes` (4 MiB). Nothing bounded the **outbound** side.

The retrieval surface has its own 128 KiB envelope budget with a `response_truncated` marker (`boundedRetrievalJSONPayload`). The ~25 graph, semantic, status and pattern tools have nothing. `limit` is a declared argument the calling agent picks, so an ordinary call can hand the client a result orders of magnitude past the frame cap — one tool call is enough to blow an agent's context or wedge the host.

## Measured, not theorised

Against the built binary on this repository's own index (40,818 symbols, 131,677 relations), one `tools/call` result:

| call | result bytes |
|---|---|
| `brain_impact` limit=10000 depth=10000 details=true | **74,044,149** |
| `brain_context` limit=10000 details=true | 12,845,400 |
| `brain_query_graph` limit=10000 | 11,532,839 |
| `brain_search_code` limit=10000 details=true | 4,034,284 |
| `brain_tests` limit=10000 details=true | 4,214,157 |
| `brain_dead_code` limit=10000 | 2,644,981 |

At `limit=1000000` (what `main` accepts today) `brain_impact` reaches **89,470,762 bytes**. Defaults are fine — `brain_impact` with no `limit` is 39,754 bytes — so this is about what a declared argument permits, not about normal use.

**This is not closed by #117/#156.** 10000 is exactly the ceiling those PRs propose; the table above is measured at that ceiling.

It also needs no corpus. The tool's output is JSON-escaped a second time when it goes into the MCP text envelope, so a request the server accepts produces a response frame roughly twice its size: a 3.0 MB `brain_search` request came back as a **6.0 MB** frame — larger than a frame the same server would refuse to read.

## The change

Route the single result-construction site through `mcpToolTextResult`, which bounds the assembled frame at the same `maxMCPFrameBytes` the reader enforces and otherwise refuses with an error naming the cap and how to narrow the request.

- The bound is on the **frame**, not the raw text, so escaping and the envelope are counted — measured with the existing `mcpToolResultTransportSize`.
- A body already over the cap short-circuits, so a 74 MB payload is not re-serialized just to measure it.
- A refusal is recoverable: the caller lowers `limit` or drops `details` and asks again. An unbounded frame is not.

Reusing `maxMCPFrameBytes` rather than inventing a number is deliberate — the server should not emit what it would not accept. Row-wise truncation with a `response_truncated` marker, as the retrieval surface does, is the richer follow-up; this closes the hole without changing what any in-budget tool returns.

## Tests

- `TestMCPToolResultRefusesAFrameTheServerWouldNotRead` — refuses an over-cap body, names the tool and the cap, refuses a body that only exceeds the cap once escaped (so measuring raw text alone would not do), and still emits a small result unchanged.
- `TestMCPToolCallEnforcesTheResultFrameCap` — drives it through the real `tools/call` path using the escape amplification above, and asserts the emitted frame stays under the cap.

Mutation-verified: replacing the bound with `return result, nil` compiles and fails both tests, one of them with `server emitted a 4456621 byte frame, over the 4194304 byte cap it enforces on reads`; restoring passes.

## Gating

Run locally — the org's Actions billing limit was reached, so CI may not start.

- `go test ./internal/cli -run TestMCP -count=1` — 58 passed
- `go test ./internal/cli -run 'TestMCP|TestRetrieval|TestBrain|TestSemantic|TestWorkspace' -count=1` — 692 passed, 1 unrelated pre-existing flake (`TestBrainBriefGitIntentLiveShapedOperationalRecall`, `fatal: could not parse HEAD`, passes 3/3 in isolation both with and without this change)
- `gofmt`, `go vet ./internal/cli` clean

## Scope

Result envelope only. Complements rather than duplicates #117/#156 (argument ceilings) — those bound the input, this bounds the output. No overlap with #118, #133, #157, #158, #185, #186.

PR 132 fix(seed): bound the reads a refresh performs over repo files https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/132
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/60
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

**Severity: MED (memory exhaustion on a normal code path).** `refresh` slurped whole repo files into memory to hash them and scan for NUL. A high-signal doc over `max-file-bytes` is deliberately *kept* (marked truncated) with only its first `max-file-bytes` copied — so the read was unbounded even though the output was bounded. An ordinary refresh allocated the full size of the largest doc in the repo, attacker- or accident-controlled.

**Fix:** hash incrementally while detecting NUL in the same pass, so the recorded digest stays **byte-identical** and only one buffer is ever held. PR 129 fix(brainwire): reject case-folded contract keys in canonical form https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/129
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/57
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

Canonical form passes unknown members through on purpose (ADR 0001, additive-only: an older verifier must be able to canonicalize and verify a **newer** producer's artifact). "Unknown" was decided by **exact** match against the contract keys — but Go's `encoding/json` matches object members to struct fields **case-insensitively**.

So a member like `manIfest` is unknown to this canonicalizer and **is** the manifest to `encoding/json`. The same signed bytes then carry two different meanings depending on which decoder reads them:

```go
raw := `{"manIfest":{"repo_key":"EVIL","generated_at":"2026-01-02T03:04:05Z","brain_schema_version":"1.0"}}`

json.Unmarshal(raw, &BrainArtifact{})   // RepoKey == "EVIL"
CanonicalUnmarshal(raw, &artifact)      // RepoKey == ""      (zero-filled)
```

and `VerifyBytes` accepts the bytes either way, because canonicalization preserves the unknown key verbatim. One signature, two readings, decided by the consumer's parser rather than by the signer.

This is the same class of cross-parser differential `canonical.go` already rejects duplicate members for, and it is not hypothetical: the artifact is consumed across a repo boundary (`entire-api`) by a Go decoder this repo does not control.

## The fix

`normalizeObject` rejects an unknown member that case-folds to a contract field. Every contract key is lowercase ASCII, so no legitimate artifact carries one. Genuinely unknown newer-minor fields still pass through untouched, and canonical form is still a fixed point over them — `TestUnknownFieldsStillPassThrough` pins both. Unknown keys are visited in sorted order so input with several collisions produces a deterministic error.

`strings.EqualFold` is a superset of `encoding/json`'s own fold matching for ASCII contract keys, so nothing the decoder would fold slips past.

## How it was found

`FuzzUnknownFieldsCannotSmuggle`, which states the ADR 0001 obligation as a testable property: for any two byte strings that verify under the same signature, the decoded `BrainArtifact` must be identical. It failed in ~3 s. The minimized input ships as a seed corpus entry (inert until that harness lands in the fuzz-targets PR).

`TestCanonicalizeRejectsCaseFoldedContractKeys` and `TestSignedArtifactCannotBeReinterpretedByFolding` are the standalone regressions; the latter reproduces the full smuggling scenario end to end.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/...`, `gofmt -l`, and `go test ./internal/brainwire/` (173 tests) — all green. Post-fix, `FuzzUnknownFieldsCannotSmuggle` ran 11.0M execs and `FuzzVerifyBytesRejectsTamper` 19.8M execs with no crasher. The full suite was not run on this host: it is under heavy load from a parallel audit fleet and long runs are timing out environmentally.

PR 128 fix(factmerge): stop the fact-set writer emitting lines its own reader rejects https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/128
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/56
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

`ParseNDJSON` scanned with a 64 KiB line bound. `WriteNDJSON` enforced nothing. A fact whose serialized record exceeded that bound wrote cleanly and then failed to load:

```
bufio.Scanner: token too long
```

So the store could persist a fact-set it could not read back — with no position and no bound in the error to act on.

On the shared cross-member head this is worse than local corruption. `factsync.Sync` parses the pulled blob with `ParseNDJSON`, so **one** member's oversized fact permanently fails **every other** member's sync, and the affected members cannot repair it, because the fact only exists on the head they cannot read.

## The fix

- `MaxLineBytes` is **16 MiB**, matching the ceiling the rest of the brain applies to untrusted inputs it reads whole (`safe_read.go`).
- `WriteNDJSON` refuses a record whose line would exceed it (`ErrRecordTooLarge`), so the two halves can never disagree again. Nothing is written when it refuses.
- An oversized line already on disk is reported as a `*ParseError` naming the line number and the bound, not as an opaque `bufio` error.

## How it was found

`FuzzNDJSONWriteReadRoundTrip`, which asserts the property directly: any record the store is willing to write, the reader must be able to read back. It failed on the first non-trivial size. The minimized input ships as a seed corpus entry (inert until that harness lands in the fuzz-targets PR).

`TestWriteReadRoundTripAtRealisticSizes`, `TestWriteRefusesUnreadableRecord`, and `TestParseReportsOversizedLineWithPosition` are the standalone regressions.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/...`, `gofmt -l`, and `go test ./internal/factmerge/ ./internal/factsync/` — all green. The full suite was not run on this host: it is under heavy load from a parallel audit fleet and long runs are timing out environmentally.

  kind=snapshot  ref=<commit>     -> semantic snapshot NDJSON: {"symbol":"Foo","kind":"func"}
  kind=overlay   ref=<base>..<head> -> {"base":...,"head":...,"branch":"feature/x"}
  kind=facts     ref=main         -> durable fact text: {"branch":"main","text":"the repo uses go"}
```

```

POST .../api/v1/repos/{id}/brain/facts/advance                Authorization: Bearer <token>
     body.data (303 bytes) = the merged fact-set NDJSON, in the clear:
       {"id":"fact:60e95c57ed6370b3f79e74a5","paths":["ops.deploy.secret"],
        "text":"the prod deploy key lives in vault path kv/prod/deploy","branch":"main",
        "origin":"distilled","status":"active","provenance":[{"session_id":"session-EV"}],
        "created_at":...,"updated_at":...}
GET  .../api/v1/repos/{id}/brain/facts/proposals?branch=main  Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

## The fix

New `internal/apiurl` — one validator, no I/O of any kind (no DNS, no disk, no network), so callers run it as their first act after resolving the flag/env and every refusal is egress-free:

- `https://` — always allowed.
- `http://` — allowed **only** when the URL's literal host is loopback (`127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`, `localhost`). PR 123 fix(semantic): a newer entire-graph minor is ingested in silence, so the index is quietly less complete than the snapshot https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/123
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/51
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Impact

ADR 0001 (`docs/adr/0001-ga-schema-contract.md` in entire-graph) states the tolerant-reader duty this consumer owes:

> Consumers ignore unknown fields within a supported major, and **warn (not fail) when they see a newer supported-major minor**, since additive facts may have been skipped.
> `entire-brain` ingestion MUST follow the tolerant-reader rules above: accept any `1.x`, ignore unknown fields, warn on a newer minor.

`validateSemanticSchema` (`internal/cli/semantic.go`) implemented only half of that:

```go
major, _, ok := strings.Cut(version, ".")
if !ok { return fmt.Errorf("unsupported semantic schema version %q", version) }
if major != semanticSupportedMajor { return fmt.Errorf("unsupported semantic schema major version %q", major) }
return nil
```

Three defects:

1. **No newer-minor warning anywhere.** A `1.2` snapshot from a newer entire-graph is accepted in silence. The resulting index is quietly less complete than the snapshot it came from — additive facts this build cannot ingest are dropped with nothing recorded. That is precisely the case the ADR requires a warning for. (`brainwire.CheckCompatibility`, `internal/brainwire/version.go:36`, implements the same ADR policy correctly one layer over; this path did not reuse it.)
2. **Only the text before the first dot is examined,** so `"1.abc"` and `"1."` are accepted as ordinary 1.x minors and a malformed header rides straight into the store.
3. **The rejection message never says what this build supports** — only what it received — collapsing "upgrade the provider" and "upgrade the brain" into one unactionable string.

## Fix

- `parseSemanticSchemaVersion` requires a well-formed `major.minor` (a trailing patch component is tolerated and ignored, since refusing it would itself violate the tolerant-reader rule).
- `validateSemanticSchema` keeps the major as the compatibility boundary and now names the supported range in every rejection.
- `semanticSchemaMinorSkewWarning` emits `provider_schema_newer_minor` for a newer minor within the supported major, naming both versions and the remedy.

### Applied at every point a provider `schema_version` crosses into this build

Recording the warning at index time alone is not enough — each of these is an independent way for an under-ingested snapshot to be trusted as complete:

| site | sink |
|---|---|
| `runSemanticIndex` | live `entire graph snapshot` header → warning recorded on the persisted manifest |
| `semanticStaleReport` | the `provider` freshness axis read by `brain doctor`/`status` and every semantic query/context/impact/changes/boundary/tests command → **degraded**, not a clean `ok` |
| `validateImportedBundle` | imported bundle manifest → warning appended to the semantic source that is then persisted |

`semanticSchemaMinorSkewWarning` is the single implementation behind all three. `validateSemanticSchema` remains the sole authority on rejecting an unparseable or unsupported-major version, and runs first at each site.

> Supersedes #120, which wired the same three sinks behind a weaker parser (`validateSemanticSchema` left lenient, and a minor parse that silently gave up on `1.2.3`). This PR carries the union: #123's strict parser plus #120's full call-site coverage. #120 is closed.

## Verification

- `TestValidateSemanticSchemaFollowsTheTolerantReaderContract` — accept `1.0`/`1.1`/`1.2`/`1.17`/`1.2.3`; refuse `""`/`1`/`2.0`/`0.9`/`1.abc`/`1.`/`x.1`.
- `TestSemanticSchemaNewerMinorWarns`, `TestSemanticSchemaErrorsNameTheSupportedRange`.
- One positive and one negative test per sink: `TestSemanticIndexRecordsNewerMinorWarning`; `TestSemanticStaleReportDegradesOnNewerMinor` / `TestSemanticStaleReportSilentAtSupportedMinor`; `TestBundleImportRecordsNewerMinorWarning` / `TestBundleImportSilentAtSupportedMinor`.
- **Mutation-verified per site:** disabling the warning at each of the three sites in turn fails exactly one test — index → `TestSemanticIndexRecordsNewerMinorWarning`, stale-report → `TestSemanticStaleReportDegradesOnNewerMinor`, bundle-import → `TestBundleImportRecordsNewerMinorWarning`. Restoring the lenient major-only parse, computing the warning but dropping it, and stripping the supported range from the message each also fail a test.
- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/cli/`, `go test ./internal/cli/` (2413 tests, green).

### Known gap, deliberately out of scope

`readSemanticSnapshotSummary` also calls `validateSemanticSchema` on a snapshot header, but it is a pure read helper returning `(semanticHeader, semanticCounts, error)` with no warning sink, and it only re-reads a snapshot whose manifest was already warned on at one of the three sites above. Wiring it needs a signature change and is not required for ADR 0001 compliance here.

https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/47
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Finding

`internal/hostedbrain/client.go:116` built the brain MCP endpoint by raw string concatenation:

```go
url := strings.TrimRight(c.BaseURL, "/") + "/api/v1/repos/" + repoID + "/brain/mcp"
```

`repoID` was not escaped. Every sibling call in the repo already escapes it — `internal/factsync/httpserver.go:63,107`, `internal/factsync/httpproposals.go:46,105,252`, `internal/cli/publish.go:534` all use `url.PathEscape`. This was the one that did not, so it was an oversight rather than a convention.

## Proof

An `httptest` server recording the request target, driven through `Client.Initialize`, observes the request going somewhere other than the brain MCP route (unfixed code):

| repo id | observed path | observed query |
|---|---|---|
| `a/b` | `/api/v1/repos/a/b/brain/mcp` | — |
| `../../admin` | `/api/v1/repos/../../admin/brain/mcp` | — |
| `..%2f..%2fadmin` | `/api/v1/repos/../../admin/brain/mcp` | — |
| `x?admin=1` | `/api/v1/repos/x` | `admin=1/brain/mcp` |
| `x#frag` | `/api/v1/repos/x` | — |
| `x/brain/facts/advance` | `/api/v1/repos/x/brain/facts/advance/brain/mcp` | — |

The `?` and `#` cases are the sharpest: the POST — carrying the member's `Authorization: Bearer` token — lands on `/api/v1/repos/x`, a different endpoint entirely, and the rest of the intended path is smuggled into the query string. `url.PathEscape(repoID)`, matching the siblings. The local variable is renamed `endpoint` (as in `publish.go`) so it no longer shadows the `net/url` package.

`TestRPCEscapesRepoID` asserts, for each payload above plus a benign id, that the server sees the `/api/v1/repos/` prefix and `/brain/mcp` suffix intact with the repo id occupying exactly one path segment and no query string smuggled out of it. It asserts on `r.URL.EscapedPath()`, which is what an HTTP router matches on, so a percent-encoded separator is correctly seen as staying inside one segment.

Mutation-verified: reverting the one-line fix fails 6 of the 7 subtests; restoring it passes all 7.

## Verification

`gofmt -l .` clean, `go vet ./...` clean, `go build ./...` clean, `go test ./internal/hostedbrain/...` green.

PR 115 fix(entityindex): do not index a shallow clone's boundary as a root commit https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/115
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/43
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

A graft truncates `git log --format=%P`, so in a shallow clone the boundary commit reports **no parents** and is indistinguishable from a real root to the walk:

```
$ git clone --depth=1 file://origin clone && cd clone
$ git log -1 --format=%P            # empty
$ git cat-file commit HEAD | head -2
tree   b7130d30b0ce47edf9a8f30a0a38d3c22f953d5e
parent ab142df864ba9d51317289381fc969732e35baa4   # the parent is right there
```

A root commit is diffed against the empty tree so its entities are recorded as `added`. The boundary therefore gets a forward delta document declaring that it **added every entity in the whole tree**, plus one reverse-index entry per entity pointing at it.

Nothing errors and nothing warns. Those records are durable git-meta, and from then on `entities history` answers "this symbol was introduced by `<boundary>`" — naming a commit that introduced none of them. The same join is what fact provenance anchors to, so the fabricated commit propagates into stored facts.

Any CI checkout (`actions/checkout` defaults to `fetch-depth: 1`) or any `git clone --depth=N` hits this.

## Repro

`internal/entityindex/build_shallow_test.go` makes a real 3-commit origin, `git clone --depth=2` off it, verifies the boundary really is grafted (`%P` empty), and indexes the clone.

```
$ go test ./internal/entityindex/ -run TestBuildDoesNotTreatAShallowBoundaryAsARootCommit -v
```

On `main`:

```
    build_shallow_test.go:142: the shallow boundary 3a000de3 was indexed against the empty tree:
    base=4b825dc6 entities=[{Change:added Kind:function Name:fn_first ... Path:first.go ...}
    {Change:added Kind:function Name:fn_second ... Path:second.go ...}]
--- FAIL: TestBuildDoesNotTreatAShallowBoundaryAsARootCommit (4.08s)
```

`first.go` was added three commits before the boundary, in history this clone does not have.

## Fix

A shallow boundary is not a root: its parent exists, it is just not in this clone, so its delta genuinely cannot be computed. Treat it as the hole it is — exactly the way a commit the provider could not diff is already treated. Nothing is written for it, no cursor steps over it (so the window keeps its "every first-parent commit from floor to tip carries a document" claim honest), and the pass reports it in `Warnings`.

Telling a boundary from a root is one `cat-file commit`: the raw object still carries its parent lines even when the graft hides them from `%P`. The check only runs for commits the walk reported as parentless, and `rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` is memoized per pass, so a full clone pays one extra `git rev-parse` at most and a repository with no parentless commits in range pays nothing at all.

The tradeoff, stated plainly: a `--depth=1` clone now indexes nothing rather than indexing one fabricated document. That is the correct direction for a store whose contents are durable and feed provenance — a deeper clone indexes everything except its boundary, which is exactly right.

## Mutation check

With the fix in place, disabling the guard (`if false && commit.Parent == "" && b.isGraftedBoundary(...)`) makes the new test fail again with the identical "indexed against the empty tree" message. The other 23 tests in the package still pass.

PR 105 fix(entityindex): keep a renamed entity's history under its current name https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/105
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/33
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

The reverse index records a commit under the entity's **post-change** key, and the alias record points `old key -> new key`. So everything a symbol did before a rename or a move lives under its *old* key, and the rename commit itself is the first entry under the new one.

Resolution only ever followed that chain forward (`AliasChain`), which means the answer depends on which spelling you happen to ask by:

- ask by the **old** key -> the full history
- ask by the **current** key -> the rename/move commit, alone

The current key is the only spelling that still exists in the tree, so it is the one a human types and the one a ranked search returns. `entities history` and `brain_entity_history` therefore print a short, plausible, wrong history for every renamed or moved symbol, with nothing anywhere reporting that anything was dropped — "this function was first touched in the commit that moved it" is wrong in the direction that looks right.

## Repro

`internal/entityindex/query_alias_family_test.go` builds a real repository (`git mv internal/pay/charge.go internal/billing/charge.go` after two commits), indexes it, then asks for the same entity by both spellings.

```
$ go test ./internal/entityindex/ -run TestCommitsByCurrentKeyKeepThePreRenameHistory -v
```

On `main`:

```
    query_alias_family_test.go:155: history depends on the spelling asked by:
          current key internal/billing/charge.go#function#fn_charge -> [806d8850f0c0bb9ce6f3518327a03e6857419ede]
          old key     internal/pay/charge.go#function#fn_charge -> [b1497049f78d22b724a01138cc669b9068619af0 753dbe598088443d3e09842d4e443d14dff484ce 806d8850f0c0bb9ce6f3518327a03e6857419ede]
--- FAIL: TestCommitsByCurrentKeyKeepThePreRenameHistory (4.26s)
```

The test also goes through `Snapshot.Search`, which is the surface the CLI and the MCP tool actually call.

## Fix

Resolve the whole alias **family** rather than the forward chain: the earlier spellings that resolve *into* a key as well as the chain forward from it. `AliasFamily` walks both directions breadth-first with a visited set, so:

- a symbol renamed and then renamed back (`A -> B -> A`) terminates instead of looping,
- predecessors are sorted at every level, so the result is deterministic (pinned by `TestAliasFamilyIsTotalAndDeterministic`, including 25 repeated calls and a two-old-keys-into-one-current-key fold),
- the family is bounded by the alias map itself rather than by a hop budget that could silently clip a long chain,
- a linear chain still comes out oldest-spelling-first.

Both call sites move over: `Snapshot.Commits` and `entityHistory` in `internal/cli/entities_cmd.go`. `AliasChain` is removed rather than left sitting beside `AliasFamily` — it had no remaining caller, and a forward-only chain is the exact shape of this bug.

## Mutation check

With the fix in place, replacing the backward frontier seed (`frontier := []string{entityKey}` -> `var frontier []string`) makes both new tests fail again — the real-git one with the same "history depends on the spelling asked by" output, and the unit one on the `A -> B -> A` cycle. The rest of the package (and `internal/cli`) still passes, so the tests pin the backward walk specifically.


PR 98 fix(entityindex): stop the window claiming a second-parent tip's chain https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/98
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/26
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

The indexed window is the index's coverage claim: *every first-parent commit from `floor` to `tip` inclusive carries a forward delta document*. A freshness tick extends the tip by walking `<tip>..<head>`, and the only thing guarding that walk is `git merge-base --is-ancestor`.

Ancestry is not first-parent ancestry. Take the most ordinary sequence there is:

```
git checkout feature && git merge main     # main's tip becomes M's SECOND parent
git checkout main    && git merge --ff-only feature
```

main's stored tip is now still an ancestor of the new head, so the window survives the divergence check — but the head's **first-parent** chain runs through the feature commits. `<tip>..<head>` excludes everything reachable from the tip by *any* parent, which is exactly those commits. The walk returns only the merge, the tip advances to it, and the window now claims a first-parent run containing commits that were never indexed.

Nothing errors and nothing warns. `entities backfill` prints `indexed window: <floor>..<head>`, and from then on every `entities history` / `brain_entity_history` query for a symbol that only changed in the hole answers "that entity was never touched" — confidently, and permanently, because the window says the range is already covered so no later pass ever revisits it.

## Repro

`internal/entityindex/build_firstparent_test.go` drives a real git repository (real commits, real merges, real fast-forward) and asserts the window's actual claim: walk `rev-list --first-parent <tip>` down to `<floor>` and require a forward document on every commit.

```
$ go test ./internal/entityindex/ -run TestBuildDoesNotClaimCoverageOverASecondParentTip -v
```

On `main`:

```
    build_firstparent_test.go:195: window 97cbfd46..cbae47a7 claims coverage but 4b153ff1 has no
    forward delta document (first-parent chain [cbae47a7f1475d4b7c7f9f1eaca973292ec71d04
    4b153ff1e993869a1b6cac6619701ef2146e62c0 3dc545894ca1b75b674ff62c4b9b93f74102102e
    97cbfd46eb920f3bb425d59d0770a3271eff94af])
--- FAIL: TestBuildDoesNotClaimCoverageOverASecondParentTip (6.98s)
```

Two of the four commits the window claims have no delta document at all.

## Fix

Check contiguity using data the walk has already parsed. `walkForward` bounds the range from the **newest** end (it counts first, then skips past what the budget cannot reach), so its oldest element is always the oldest commit of the range — and when the range really does sit on top of the tip, that commit's first parent *is* the tip.

`contiguousWithTip` asserts exactly that. When it fails, the tip is not on the head's first-parent chain, so the walk cannot be used to advance the cursor: drop the window and re-cover from the head, which is the path a diverged tip already takes. An empty range with `tip != head` means the same thing and is treated the same way — if the tip were on the head's first-parent chain there would be at least one commit above it, and no commit above the tip is reachable from it.

The repair is cheap: `alreadyIndexed` skips every commit that already has a document, so re-covering costs one probe per commit, not one `graph diff` per commit.

## Mutation check

With the fix in place, replacing `return commits[0].Parent == tip` with `return true` makes the new test fail again with the identical "claims coverage but ... has no forward delta document" message. The other 23 tests in the package still pass, so the test is pinning the check itself rather than something incidental.

PR 89 One-command onboarding: install from git, then `entire brain setup` https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/89

https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/17
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

One command per machine, one per repository. `entire brain setup` builds a queryable
brain in about a second, and this PR is mostly the work of making that true for a person
who has never seen the tool before.

## The journey, verified end to end

```sh
# once per machine
git clone https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain.git
entire-brain/scripts/install.sh

# once per repository
cd /path/to/your/repo
entire brain setup
```

Run on a clean clone at `52a4bf81` (this branch merged with `main`), against a fresh
`git init` repository with **no remote** — the shape that used to fail:

```
Brain ready in 870ms
  repo        /Users/…/proj  (local/proj-966f22b7fb9b)
  instant     + sessions  + seed  + history  + docs  + semantic  + patterns  + entities  + memory  (840ms)
  facts       .............. 0/0 sessions distilled
  workspace   + default  (30ms)
  daemon      - skipped: --no-daemon  (0s)

Next
  entire brain overview        what this project is
  entire brain brief "<task>"  task-shaped context
  entire brain status          backfill progress and daemon health
```

`install.sh` 5.4s · `setup` 870ms · `status`, `overview`, `brief` all exit 0 ·
`brief` returns repo-derived content (`symbol Greet greet/greet.go:3-8`).

## What was broken

Every item below was found by **running the product as a user**, not by reading it. The
demo scripts in this PR passed clean and caught none of the first six.

### Nobody could install it

`scripts/install.sh` hardcoded `../entire-graph`, and the README said outright *"The
directory names matter."* Clone one repo, rename a directory, or work from a worktree and
you hit a dead end. It now resolves the provider three ways — explicit `ENTIRE_GRAPH_DIR`,
a discovered checkout **verified by content rather than by folder name**, or a shallow
clone from git — and `scripts/bootstrap.sh` covers starting from nothing. Preflight
reports every missing prerequisite at once instead of dying on the first, partway through
a build.

Piped-curl was considered and rejected: this repo is private, so `curl | sh` would mean
"export a token, then pipe an unread script into your shell", and the install is a source
build so the clone happens either way.

### The docs stopped at the install

`README.md` said *"That is the whole install"* and never mentioned `entire brain setup`.
`docs/getting-started.md` mentioned it **zero times in 762 lines** — it sent readers to
`refresh` instead. A person finished with working plugins and no idea what to do in their
own repository.

The old prerequisites were also wrong, which the code settles: `setup` needs **a git
repository** and nothing else. `entire enable` is not required, and `setup` deliberately
will not do it — from `setup_status.go`, *"hook registration belongs to the Entire CLI's
repository enablement … Duplicating it here would produce two hooks racing to distill the
same session."*

### `entire enable` and `entire brain setup` do not compose

`enable` writes `.entire/` and `.claude/` and **leaves them uncommitted**, so the very
next `setup` refuses to seed or index a dirty worktree — two red ✗ caused by the command
directly above it. The real order is `enable` → **commit** → `setup`, now documented with
the reason, and the refusal carries a remedy that names a flag `setup` actually accepts.

### A fresh repository always failed the semantic component

```
x semantic index: repo key mismatch: semantic snapshot repo_key "local/myproject"
                  does not match current repo "local/myproject-459a916099fb"
```

`entire-brain` derives `<base>-sha256(abspath)[:12]`; `entire-graph` recognises only
github.com remotes and otherwise falls back to `local/<basename>`. Measured per origin:

| origin | provider | brain | |
|---|---|---|---|
| none | `local/proj` | `local/proj-<12hex>` | mismatch |
| github | `gh/acme/proj` | `gh/acme/proj` | match |
| gitlab | `local/gl-proj` | `gl/acme/gl-proj` | mismatch |
| bitbucket | `local/bb-proj` | `bb/acme/bb-proj` | mismatch |

So it was never "no remote" — **every non-GitHub origin** hit it, while the hint told
repositories that already had a remote to add one, blaming the reader for a disagreement
between two of our own tools.

Fixed on the live path only: the brain accepts the provider's own fallback spelling of the
directory it just handed that provider, and stores the snapshot under its own key. Bundle
import and stored-snapshot read-back still compare keys exactly. This is not a weakened
guard — the live path validates commit and tree against HEAD immediately afterwards, and
key equality was only ever asserting that two tools spell a name alike.

Two alternatives were rejected for cause: dropping brain's suffix merges two same-basename
repositories' brains, and making the provider adopt the suffix invalidates every existing
index, because its repo key is baked into every `symbolID()`.

### `setup` recommended a command it had just broken

`setup` reused the watch tick's `historyIndex:false` — correct for a five-minute tick,
wrong for one-shot onboarding — so the first `brief` after the first `setup` printed
*"history index missing"* and silently dropped its transcript half.

### The output answered in the wrong vocabulary

You typed `entire brain setup`; the Next block replied `entire-brain overview`. Output now
follows how you invoked it, keyed on `ENTIRE_CLI_VERSION`, swept across every hint, error
and follow-up.

`entire checkpoint list` pages its output, and nothing set `PAGER`, so under a captured

PR 190 fix(semantic): read a relation endpoint's path out of the ID correctly https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/190
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/111
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## The bug

`semanticEndpointPath` derived a file path from a semantic relation endpoint ID with `strings.Split(id, ":")` and returned `parts[2]`. That path is what `.brainignore` is matched against.

entire-graph builds endpoint IDs by joining **unescaped** fields with `":"`:

```
symbol:   <repo-key>:<language>:<path>:<kind>:<qualified-name>
file:     <repo-key>:file:<path>
external: external:<kind>:<value>
```

Three of those fields may legitimately contain `":"` — a file path (`od:d/mod.py`), a local repo key (`local/<directory name>`), and a qualified name (an Express route symbol is named `/users/:id`). So the fixed-index read landed on the wrong segment:

| case | endpoint | path read |
|---|---|---|
| ordinary | `main.go` | `main.go` — ok |
| colon in the **file path**, ordinary repo | `od:d/mod.py` | `od` — wrong |
| colon in the **repo key** | `main.go` | `Go` — wrong |

**No unusual directory name is needed.** An ordinary GitHub-keyed repo containing a file at `od:d/mod.py` is enough, and the `len(parts) < 5` guard does not fire (that ID splits into six fields).

### Two data-integrity consequences

1. **Relations redacted for files that are not ignored.** With a `.brainignore` rule for the directory `od`, `od:d/mod.py` is correctly kept — the file record and its symbols survive, because those are filtered by their real `file_path`. But every relation touching them was dropped, because the endpoint parse read `"od"`. One-sided, silent loss of the relation graph for a file the user never asked to hide. The stock ignore set (`build`, `vendor`, `dist`, `target`, `node_modules`) reaches this with no `.brainignore` at all: a file at `build:tools/mod.go` keeps its symbols and loses its edges.

2. **Relations kept for files that are ignored.** A file endpoint has three fields, so `len(parts) < 5` returned `""` for *every* file endpoint and skipped the check entirely. entire-graph resolves imports and co-change pairs to `<repo-key>:file:<path>` endpoints for files it emits no record for, so the ignored-ID set cannot cover them and the endpoint ID is the only signal — a relation naming `secret/config.go` went into the brain verbatim.

The function's own comment encoded the false premise ("the repo key, language, and kind segments never contain `:`, so the path is always the third field").

## The fix

A relation record has no `file_path` to read the path off: entire-graph's `RelationRecord` carries only `from_id`/`to_id`. The path has to come out of the ID, so the parse is now anchored on the two fields that are known to be free of `":"`.

- **The repo key.** The snapshot header carries it, and entire-graph builds the header field and every ID from the same value (`sc.key`), so the prefix match is exact. An endpoint carrying a different repo key names no file in this repository and now resolves to no path rather than a spurious one.
- **The kind**, which is always a bare token — no `"/"`, no `"."`.

A **file** endpoint is then exact by construction: everything after the `file:` marker is the path, colons included. A **symbol** endpoint cuts the language at the first colon and takes the first split whose kind field is a bare token — which keeps a colon in the qualified name from stealing the split (`route` is accepted before `/users/:id` can be read as a kind) while stepping over one in the path (`d/mod.py` is rejected as a kind, so `od:d/mod.py` stays whole).

Escaping or sanitising the repo key was not the fix here: the path injects colons through the same joint, so the consumer stays broken regardless.

## Tests

`internal/cli/semantic_endpoint_path_test.go`:

- `TestSemanticEndpointPathRecoversFieldsAroundColons` — 15 cases across every ID shape: colon in the path, in the repo key, in the qualified name, in the path *and* the qualified name, file endpoints with and without a colon, externals, a foreign repo key, an opaque endpoint.
- `TestSemanticIndexKeepsRelationsForColonPathOutsideIgnoredDirectory` — end to end through `runSemanticIndex` with a real `.brainignore`: a rule for `od` must not redact `od:d/mod.py`.
- `TestSemanticIndexDropsRelationsForIgnoredColonPath` — the same path, genuinely ignored, is redacted.
- `TestSemanticIndexDropsRelationsToIgnoredFileEndpoints` — relations naming ignored files only through file endpoint IDs are dropped and their paths do not appear in the persisted snapshot.
- `TestFilterSemanticSnapshotHonorsColonPathEndpoints` — the re-filter path shares the parse and reaches the same verdicts.

`TestSemanticEndpointPath` is retired in place; the new table covers all six of its cases.

**Mutation-verified.** Restoring the `strings.Split` body behind the new signature (so it still compiles) fails four of the five tests, reproducing the exact wrong values above — `"od"` for `od:d/mod.py`, `"Go"` for the colon-in-repo-key case, `""` for every file endpoint.

`go test ./internal/cli -run 'Semantic|Ignore|Relation' -count=1` green; `go vet ./...` and `gofmt` clean.

## Known residual

The kind anchor cannot separate a path whose colon-delimited tail segment is itself a bare token — a file literally named `od:README` still resolves to `od`. Closing that would mean pinning entire-graph's kind enum inside Brain, trading a contrived case for a drift hazard on every kind the provider adds. Every path shape with a `/` or a `.` after the colon — which is every path with a directory or an extension — resolves exactly.

PR 188 fix(mcp): bound brain_index_repository the way brain_refresh is bounded https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/188
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/109
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## The defect

`runMCP` serves one request at a time: read a frame, handle it to completion, write the response, read again. However long a tool call takes is time the server answers **nothing at all** — not another tool, not a host's liveness check.

`brain_refresh` already carries an MCP-scoped deadline for exactly that reason, with a comment saying so and an error pointing at the CLI. `brain_index_repository` — the one tool that walks the whole repository through an external provider, so the one most able to run long — had none. It ran on the bare request context.

## Measured

Against the built binary on this repository (40,818 symbols, 131,677 relations), three requests written back to back into the same stdio pipe:

```
t=+ 0.0s  initialize            -> answered
t=+40.0s  brain_index_repository-> answered
t=+42.3s  brain_status          -> answered
```

`brain_status` was sitting in the pipe the whole time. Nothing came back for 40 seconds. That is longer than a typical host tool-call timeout, and on a larger repository — or with a provider that wedges — there is no ceiling at all.

## The change

Wrap the index in `mcpIndexTimeout` and convert a deadline into the same shape of error `brain_refresh` returns, naming the CLI command that has no such constraint. The provider runs under `exec.CommandContext`, so the deadline actually reclaims the pipe rather than just abandoning the wait.

The value matches `mcpRefreshTimeout` deliberately: the constraint is not about how long indexing "should" take, it is about how long a single MCP call may hold the only pipe. Both are `var`s so tests can shrink them.

## Tests

`TestMCPBrainIndexRepositoryHonorsTimeout` shrinks the bound to 1ms, runs the index against a runner that blocks until its context is cancelled, and asserts both halves: the timeout is surfaced to the caller, **and the request queued behind it is then served** — the pipe came back, which is the whole point.

Mutation-verified: dropping the deadline compiles, and the test then **hangs until the Go test timeout** (`FAIL ... 60.523s`) rather than failing fast — which is precisely the defect. Restoring passes in 0.6s.

## Gating

Run locally — the org's Actions billing limit was reached, so CI may not start.

- `go test ./internal/cli -run TestMCP -count=1` — 57 passed
- `gofmt`, `go vet ./internal/cli` clean

## Scope

One tool's context. No overlap with the other open MCP PRs (#117, #118, #133, #156, #157, #158, #185, #186, #187).

Not addressed here, and noted for the record: the serial request loop itself. Making the server handle concurrent tool calls is a design change — the per-response privacy lock handoff (`mcpResponsePrivacyState`) and the brain's file locks both assume one in-flight request — so this PR bounds the worst offender rather than reworking the loop.

PR 187 fix(mcp): stop emitting a result frame the server would refuse to read https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/187
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/108
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## The defect

`readMCPMessage` rejects an **inbound** frame over `maxMCPFrameBytes` (4 MiB). Nothing bounded the **outbound** side.

The retrieval surface has its own 128 KiB envelope budget with a `response_truncated` marker (`boundedRetrievalJSONPayload`). The ~25 graph, semantic, status and pattern tools have nothing. `limit` is a declared argument the calling agent picks, so an ordinary call can hand the client a result orders of magnitude past the frame cap — one tool call is enough to blow an agent's context or wedge the host.

## Measured, not theorised

Against the built binary on this repository's own index (40,818 symbols, 131,677 relations), one `tools/call` result:

| call | result bytes |
|---|---|
| `brain_impact` limit=10000 depth=10000 details=true | **74,044,149** |
| `brain_context` limit=10000 details=true | 12,845,400 |
| `brain_query_graph` limit=10000 | 11,532,839 |
| `brain_search_code` limit=10000 details=true | 4,034,284 |
| `brain_tests` limit=10000 details=true | 4,214,157 |
| `brain_dead_code` limit=10000 | 2,644,981 |

At `limit=1000000` (what `main` accepts today) `brain_impact` reaches **89,470,762 bytes**. Defaults are fine — `brain_impact` with no `limit` is 39,754 bytes — so this is about what a declared argument permits, not about normal use.

**This is not closed by #117/#156.** 10000 is exactly the ceiling those PRs propose; the table above is measured at that ceiling.

It also needs no corpus. The tool's output is JSON-escaped a second time when it goes into the MCP text envelope, so a request the server accepts produces a response frame roughly twice its size: a 3.0 MB `brain_search` request came back as a **6.0 MB** frame — larger than a frame the same server would refuse to read.

## The change

Route the single result-construction site through `mcpToolTextResult`, which bounds the assembled frame at the same `maxMCPFrameBytes` the reader enforces and otherwise refuses with an error naming the cap and how to narrow the request.

- The bound is on the **frame**, not the raw text, so escaping and the envelope are counted — measured with the existing `mcpToolResultTransportSize`.
- A body already over the cap short-circuits, so a 74 MB payload is not re-serialized just to measure it.
- A refusal is recoverable: the caller lowers `limit` or drops `details` and asks again. An unbounded frame is not.

Reusing `maxMCPFrameBytes` rather than inventing a number is deliberate — the server should not emit what it would not accept. Row-wise truncation with a `response_truncated` marker, as the retrieval surface does, is the richer follow-up; this closes the hole without changing what any in-budget tool returns.

## Tests

- `TestMCPToolResultRefusesAFrameTheServerWouldNotRead` — refuses an over-cap body, names the tool and the cap, refuses a body that only exceeds the cap once escaped (so measuring raw text alone would not do), and still emits a small result unchanged.
- `TestMCPToolCallEnforcesTheResultFrameCap` — drives it through the real `tools/call` path using the escape amplification above, and asserts the emitted frame stays under the cap.

Mutation-verified: replacing the bound with `return result, nil` compiles and fails both tests, one of them with `server emitted a 4456621 byte frame, over the 4194304 byte cap it enforces on reads`; restoring passes.

## Gating

Run locally — the org's Actions billing limit was reached, so CI may not start.

- `go test ./internal/cli -run TestMCP -count=1` — 58 passed
- `go test ./internal/cli -run 'TestMCP|TestRetrieval|TestBrain|TestSemantic|TestWorkspace' -count=1` — 692 passed, 1 unrelated pre-existing flake (`TestBrainBriefGitIntentLiveShapedOperationalRecall`, `fatal: could not parse HEAD`, passes 3/3 in isolation both with and without this change)
- `gofmt`, `go vet ./internal/cli` clean

## Scope

Result envelope only. Complements rather than duplicates #117/#156 (argument ceilings) — those bound the input, this bounds the output. No overlap with #118, #133, #157, #158, #185, #186.

An ordinary refresh allocated the full size of the largest doc in the repo, attacker- or accident-controlled.

**Fix:** hash incrementally while detecting NUL in the same pass, so the recorded digest stays **byte-identical** and only one buffer is ever held. Manifest reads (`package.json`, `mise`) are bounded outright — a manifest is small, and a hostile or corrupt one should not exhaust memory before the parser sees it.

**Tests (3):** `inspectSeedFile`, `writeSeedDocs`, and manifest reads each asserted bounded by measured allocation.

**Mutation-verified:** reverting the two bounded manifest reads to `os.ReadFile` fails with `miseCommands allocated 174003952 bytes for a 67108864 byte manifest; want < 41943040 (the read is unbounded)`.

**Verification:** `go build ./...` clean; the three bounded-read tests pass. Full suite not re-run on a loaded host.

PR 129 fix(brainwire): reject case-folded contract keys in canonical form https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/129
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/57
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

Canonical form passes unknown members through on purpose (ADR 0001, additive-only: an older verifier must be able to canonicalize and verify a **newer** producer's artifact). "Unknown" was decided by **exact** match against the contract keys — but Go's `encoding/json` matches object members to struct fields **case-insensitively**.

So a member like `manIfest` is unknown to this canonicalizer and **is** the manifest to `encoding/json`. The same signed bytes then carry two different meanings depending on which decoder reads them:

```go
raw := `{"manIfest":{"repo_key":"EVIL","generated_at":"2026-01-02T03:04:05Z","brain_schema_version":"1.0"}}`

json.Unmarshal(raw, &BrainArtifact{})   // RepoKey == "EVIL"
CanonicalUnmarshal(raw, &artifact)      // RepoKey == ""      (zero-filled)
```

and `VerifyBytes` accepts the bytes either way, because canonicalization preserves the unknown key verbatim. One signature, two readings, decided by the consumer's parser rather than by the signer.

This is the same class of cross-parser differential `canonical.go` already rejects duplicate members for, and it is not hypothetical: the artifact is consumed across a repo boundary (`entire-api`) by a Go decoder this repo does not control.

## The fix

`normalizeObject` rejects an unknown member that case-folds to a contract field. Every contract key is lowercase ASCII, so no legitimate artifact carries one. Genuinely unknown newer-minor fields still pass through untouched, and canonical form is still a fixed point over them — `TestUnknownFieldsStillPassThrough` pins both. Unknown keys are visited in sorted order so input with several collisions produces a deterministic error.

`strings.EqualFold` is a superset of `encoding/json`'s own fold matching for ASCII contract keys, so nothing the decoder would fold slips past.

## How it was found

`FuzzUnknownFieldsCannotSmuggle`, which states the ADR 0001 obligation as a testable property: for any two byte strings that verify under the same signature, the decoded `BrainArtifact` must be identical. It failed in ~3 s. The minimized input ships as a seed corpus entry (inert until that harness lands in the fuzz-targets PR).

`TestCanonicalizeRejectsCaseFoldedContractKeys` and `TestSignedArtifactCannotBeReinterpretedByFolding` are the standalone regressions; the latter reproduces the full smuggling scenario end to end.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/...`, `gofmt -l`, and `go test ./internal/brainwire/` (173 tests) — all green. Post-fix, `FuzzUnknownFieldsCannotSmuggle` ran 11.0M execs and `FuzzVerifyBytesRejectsTamper` 19.8M execs with no crasher. The full suite was not run on this host: it is under heavy load from a parallel audit fleet and long runs are timing out environmentally.

PR 105 fix(entityindex): keep a renamed entity's history under its current name https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/105
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/33
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

The reverse index records a commit under the entity's **post-change** key, and the alias record points `old key -> new key`. So everything a symbol did before a rename or a move lives under its *old* key, and the rename commit itself is the first entry under the new one.

Resolution only ever followed that chain forward (`AliasChain`), which means the answer depends on which spelling you happen to ask by:

- ask by the **old** key -> the full history
- ask by the **current** key -> the rename/move commit, alone

The current key is the only spelling that still exists in the tree, so it is the one a human types and the one a ranked search returns. `entities history` and `brain_entity_history` therefore print a short, plausible, wrong history for every renamed or moved symbol, with nothing anywhere reporting that anything was dropped — "this function was first touched in the commit that moved it" is wrong in the direction that looks right.

## Repro

`internal/entityindex/query_alias_family_test.go` builds a real repository (`git mv internal/pay/charge.go internal/billing/charge.go` after two commits), indexes it, then asks for the same entity by both spellings.

```
$ go test ./internal/entityindex/ -run TestCommitsByCurrentKeyKeepThePreRenameHistory -v
```

On `main`:

```
    query_alias_family_test.go:155: history depends on the spelling asked by:
          current key internal/billing/charge.go#function#fn_charge -> [806d8850f0c0bb9ce6f3518327a03e6857419ede]
          old key     internal/pay/charge.go#function#fn_charge -> [b1497049f78d22b724a01138cc669b9068619af0 753dbe598088443d3e09842d4e443d14dff484ce 806d8850f0c0bb9ce6f3518327a03e6857419ede]
--- FAIL: TestCommitsByCurrentKeyKeepThePreRenameHistory (4.26s)
```

The test also goes through `Snapshot.Search`, which is the surface the CLI and the MCP tool actually call.

## Fix

Resolve the whole alias **family** rather than the forward chain: the earlier spellings that resolve *into* a key as well as the chain forward from it. `AliasFamily` walks both directions breadth-first with a visited set, so:

- a symbol renamed and then renamed back (`A -> B -> A`) terminates instead of looping,
- predecessors are sorted at every level, so the result is deterministic (pinned by `TestAliasFamilyIsTotalAndDeterministic`, including 25 repeated calls and a two-old-keys-into-one-current-key fold),
- the family is bounded by the alias map itself rather than by a hop budget that could silently clip a long chain,
- a linear chain still comes out oldest-spelling-first.

Both call sites move over: `Snapshot.Commits` and `entityHistory` in `internal/cli/entities_cmd.go`. `AliasChain` is removed rather than left sitting beside `AliasFamily` — it had no remaining caller, and a forward-only chain is the exact shape of this bug.

## Mutation check

With the fix in place, replacing the backward frontier seed (`frontier := []string{entityKey}` -> `var frontier []string`) makes both new tests fail again — the real-git one with the same "history depends on the spelling asked by" output, and the unit one on the `A -> B -> A` cycle. The rest of the package (and `internal/cli`) still passes, so the tests pin the backward walk specifically.


PR 98 fix(entityindex): stop the window claiming a second-parent tip's chain https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/98
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/26
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

The indexed window is the index's coverage claim: *every first-parent commit from `floor` to `tip` inclusive carries a forward delta document*. A freshness tick extends the tip by walking `<tip>..<head>`, and the only thing guarding that walk is `git merge-base --is-ancestor`.

Ancestry is not first-parent ancestry. Take the most ordinary sequence there is:

```
git checkout feature && git merge main     # main's tip becomes M's SECOND parent
git checkout main    && git merge --ff-only feature
```

main's stored tip is now still an ancestor of the new head, so the window survives the divergence check — but the head's **first-parent** chain runs through the feature commits. `<tip>..<head>` excludes everything reachable from the tip by *any* parent, which is exactly those commits. The walk returns only the merge, the tip advances to it, and the window now claims a first-parent run containing commits that were never indexed.

Nothing errors and nothing warns. `entities backfill` prints `indexed window: <floor>..<head>`, and from then on every `entities history` / `brain_entity_history` query for a symbol that only changed in the hole answers "that entity was never touched" — confidently, and permanently, because the window says the range is already covered so no later pass ever revisits it.

## Repro

`internal/entityindex/build_firstparent_test.go` drives a real git repository (real commits, real merges, real fast-forward) and asserts the window's actual claim: walk `rev-list --first-parent <tip>` down to `<floor>` and require a forward document on every commit.

```
$ go test ./internal/entityindex/ -run TestBuildDoesNotClaimCoverageOverASecondParentTip -v
```

On `main`:

```
    build_firstparent_test.go:195: window 97cbfd46..cbae47a7 claims coverage but 4b153ff1 has no
    forward delta document (first-parent chain [cbae47a7f1475d4b7c7f9f1eaca973292ec71d04
    4b153ff1e993869a1b6cac6619701ef2146e62c0 3dc545894ca1b75b674ff62c4b9b93f74102102e
    97cbfd46eb920f3bb425d59d0770a3271eff94af])
--- FAIL: TestBuildDoesNotClaimCoverageOverASecondParentTip (6.98s)
```

Two of the four commits the window claims have no delta document at all.

## Fix

Check contiguity using data the walk has already parsed. `walkForward` bounds the range from the **newest** end (it counts first, then skips past what the budget cannot reach), so its oldest element is always the oldest commit of the range — and when the range really does sit on top of the tip, that commit's first parent *is* the tip.

`contiguousWithTip` asserts exactly that. When it fails, the tip is not on the head's first-parent chain, so the walk cannot be used to advance the cursor: drop the window and re-cover from the head, which is the path a diverged tip already takes. An empty range with `tip != head` means the same thing and is treated the same way — if the tip were on the head's first-parent chain there would be at least one commit above it, and no commit above the tip is reachable from it.

The repair is cheap: `alreadyIndexed` skips every commit that already has a document, so re-covering costs one probe per commit, not one `graph diff` per commit.

## Mutation check

With the fix in place, replacing `return commits[0].Parent == tip` with `return true` makes the new test fail again with the identical "claims coverage but ... has no forward delta document" message. The other 23 tests in the package still pass, so the test is pinning the check itself rather than something incidental.

One command per machine, one per repository. `entire brain setup` builds a queryable
brain in about a second, and this PR is mostly the work of making that true for a person
who has never seen the tool before.

## The journey, verified end to end

```sh
# once per machine
git clone https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain.git
entire-brain/scripts/install.sh

# once per repository
cd /path/to/your/repo
entire brain setup
```

Run on a clean clone at `52a4bf81` (this branch merged with `main`), against a fresh
`git init` repository with **no remote** — the shape that used to fail:

```
Brain ready in 870ms
  repo        /Users/…/proj  (local/proj-966f22b7fb9b)
  instant     + sessions  + seed  + history  + docs  + semantic  + patterns  + entities  + memory  (840ms)
  facts       .............. 0/0 sessions distilled
  workspace   + default  (30ms)
  daemon      - skipped: --no-daemon  (0s)

Next
  entire brain overview        what this project is
  entire brain brief "<task>"  task-shaped context
  entire brain status          backfill progress and daemon health
```

`install.sh` 5.4s · `setup` 870ms · `status`, `overview`, `brief` all exit 0 ·
`brief` returns repo-derived content (`symbol Greet greet/greet.go:3-8`).

Every item below was found by **running the product as a user**, not by reading it. The
demo scripts in this PR passed clean and caught none of the first six.

### Nobody could install it

`scripts/install.sh` hardcoded `../entire-graph`, and the README said outright *"The
directory names matter."* Clone one repo, rename a directory, or work from a worktree and
you hit a dead end. It now resolves the provider three ways — explicit `ENTIRE_GRAPH_DIR`,
a discovered checkout **verified by content rather than by folder name**, or a shallow
clone from git — and `scripts/bootstrap.sh` covers starting from nothing. Preflight
reports every missing prerequisite at once instead of dying on the first, partway through
a build.

Piped-curl was considered and rejected: this repo is private, so `curl | sh` would mean
"export a token, then pipe an unread script into your shell", and the install is a source
build so the clone happens either way.

### The docs stopped at the install

`README.md` said *"That is the whole install"* and never mentioned `entire brain setup`.
`docs/getting-started.md` mentioned it **zero times in 762 lines** — it sent readers to
`refresh` instead. A person finished with working plugins and no idea what to do in their
own repository.

The old prerequisites were also wrong, which the code settles: `setup` needs **a git
repository** and nothing else. `entire enable` is not required, and `setup` deliberately
will not do it — from `setup_status.go`, *"hook registration belongs to the Entire CLI's
repository enablement … Duplicating it here would produce two hooks racing to distill the
same session."*

### `entire enable` and `entire brain setup` do not compose

`enable` writes `.entire/` and `.claude/` and **leaves them uncommitted**, so the very
next `setup` refuses to seed or index a dirty worktree — two red ✗ caused by the command
directly above it. The real order is `enable` → **commit** → `setup`, now documented with
the reason, and the refusal carries a remedy that names a flag `setup` actually accepts.

### A fresh repository always failed the semantic component

```
x semantic index: repo key mismatch: semantic snapshot repo_key "local/myproject"

```

`entire-brain` derives `<base>-sha256(abspath)[:12]`; `entire-graph` recognises only
github.com remotes and otherwise falls back to `local/<basename>`. Measured per origin:

| origin | provider | brain | |
|---|---|---|---|
| none | `local/proj` | `local/proj-<12hex>` | mismatch |
| github | `gh/acme/proj` | `gh/acme/proj` | match |
| gitlab | `local/gl-proj` | `gl/acme/gl-proj` | mismatch |
| bitbucket | `local/bb-proj` | `bb/acme/bb-proj` | mismatch |

key equality was only ever asserting that two tools spell a name alike.

wrong for one-shot onboarding — so the first `brief` after the first `setup` printed
*"history index missing"* and silently dropped its transcript half.

### The output answered in the wrong vocabulary

You typed `entire brain setup`; the Next block replied `entire-brain overview`. Output now
follows how you invoked it, keyed on `ENTIRE_CLI_VERSION`, swept across every hint, error
